transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Location: Zoom call (recording on)
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Mike (Valora CTO), Ana (Valora ML), Samir (Valora Platform), Becky (Valora Security)

Summary:
Quick hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, key generation parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff patterns and idempotency, and a short safety/data residency discussion. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a patient-facing summarization product; concerned about latency and PHI handling.

Topics Covered:
- Hosted API streaming semantics and partial tokens
- Parameter trade-offs: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
- Retries, exponential backoff, idempotency keys and best-effort dedup
- Console quick tour (usage, per-route latency breakdown) and Optimize tips for batching/quantization recommendations
- Security basics: SOC2 link, KMS, data retention, VPC/private deployment options (brief)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — looks like we've got... um, about 40 minutes. Quick intro: I'm Jordan, AE. With me are Priya and Liam on the technical side. Could you do quick intros?
[00:12] Mike (Valora): Yeah hi, Mike - CTO at Valora. We're looking into how to host summaries for patient messages with low latency, and want to see how your hosted API behaves.
[00:20] Ana (Valora): Ana, ML lead — especially interested in streaming behaviour and stopping tokens cleanly.
[00:26] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. We'll do a short overview, live demo of a chat gen call and streaming, then go into retries and safety questions. Sound good?
[00:33] Mike: Yep. Also Becky from security is on to ask about data retention — she'll speak up when needed.
[00:38] Becky (Valora): Hey, thanks.

[00:45] Priya: Alright jumping in — first high-level: hosted API supports streaming responses for chat and generation endpoints. Streaming returns partial deltas and we commit tokens as they arrive. The console shows per-route latency and token counts right?
[00:58] Jordan: Yep — the Console has a per-model dashboard. One note: there can be small variations in chunk sizes depending on model and sequence length, we show that in the traces.
[01:12] Ana: When you say "partial deltas" do you mean the API returns text chunks or token deltas? How do you suggest we assemble?
[01:20] Priya: Good q — the stream sends text deltas; typically clients append in order. We recommend an incremental rendering approach so UI can show partials. Also include an idempotency key per high-level user interaction to help with retries.
[01:35] Samir (Valora): Does the stream guarantee order? If we drop a packet and re-request, could we get duplicates?
[01:42] Liam (Redwood SE): The stream itself is ordered over the connection. If a client reconnects and replays a request, duplicates are possible — so idempotency and dedup logic client-side is recommended. For hosted we also have server-side best-effort de-dup when idempotency keys are present, but it's not strict once network reconnection happens.
[02:05] Mike: What's the typical latency for short summaries, like 100 tokens?
[02:10] Priya: For our curated open models we see 50-150ms per token on a steady-state for 8k context models under normal load; first token latency is usually higher due to setup. In hosted we'll Surface percentiles in the Console — p50/p95.
[02:28] Ana: Are there any knobs to tune to reduce latency? e.g., smaller batch sizes, quantization?
[02:34] Priya: Yes - Optimize will recommend quantization profiles and batching configurations by workload. For synchronous low-latency, reduce lookahead and batch windows. Also pick model variants with lower compute, e.g., 1.5B vs 7B.

[02:50] Jordan: Let me share my screen — we'll run a simple chat generation. You'll see the streaming chunks in the terminal and the console on the other tab.
[03:00] [screen share starts; live demo]
[03:12] Priya: Ok I'm sending a message: "Summarize this patient message in 2-3 bullets, remove PHI". Using temp=0.2, top_p=0.95, max_tokens=120. Streaming on.
[03:28] [00:03:28] Priya (Redwood SE): (typing) starting the request...
[03:35] [00:03:35] Terminal stream: "Patient reports chest pain and shortness of breath..." (partial)
[03:48] Ana: Looks good — partial arrives quickly. How do you handle stop sequences? If one of our patients' templates includes '---' as delimiter, can we pass a stop sequence?
[03:58] Priya: Yes, stop sequences are supported. When the model emits a stop token the stream closes with final delta. Note: depending on model tokenization stop markers may be split so we recommend post-filtering on the client too.
[04:12] Samir: And the token accounting — is streaming tokenized at generation time or after? We need accurate cost estimates.
[04:20] Jordan: Token accounting is done server-side as tokens are generated. The Console and usage API report tokens consumed per request; billing is based on completed tokens at the end of the request. If a retry happens, idempotency keys prevent double billing in many cases, but it's good to check the transaction IDs in usage logs.

[04:40] Priya: Next: retries. If the request times out or you see a 5xx, recommended pattern is exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 retries for idempotent operations. For non-idempotent (like streaming where client-side partial state exists) we suggest a full re-run only if you can dedup or the UI can rehydrate.
[05:00] Mike: Can you walk through a concrete retry flow — say network drops halfway through streaming?
[05:06] Priya: Sure — common approach: you attach an idempotency-key header per prompt exchange. If you reconnect and the server has a recorded completed response for that key, you'll get the final result. If the server didn't finish, you may get a 202 or start a fresh run. Also store the last completed chunk id and resume logic in UI.
[05:28] Becky: From security side, what happens to the content? We can't store PHI in logs. Is there an option to disable request logging?
[05:36] Jordan: Good point — hosted API has configurable retention. For enterprise customers we can turn off long-term logs and integrate with their KMS for encrypt-at-rest. We'll share the security whitepaper and SOC2 link. Also private deployment (VPC or on-prem) is an option if you need full control of logs.
[05:54] Becky: Also SSO and audit logs?
[05:58] Liam: We support SAML SSO, RBAC and audit logs via the Console. Audit logs can be exported to their bucket. We'll flag the specific audit events you asked for in the follow-up.

[06:15] Ana: Back to params — how aggressive should we set temperature for deterministic summaries? 0.0 is safe?
[06:22] Priya: Temperature=0 is deterministic-ish but some models still have non-determinism with beam sampling architecture. We recommend 0.0-0.2 for clinical summarization. Also set top_p low (like 0.9) and include strong stop sequences.
[06:38] Mike: If we put temp=0, do we risk repeated phrasing across users? Any diversity tradeoffs?
[06:44] Priya: Yes, lower temp reduces diversity; for user-facing summaries lower is desirable to keep consistent messaging. You can also apply post-processing templates to standardize phrasing.

[07:00] Jordan: Quick Console tour — here's the route page, latency histogram, tokens by user, and per-token cost breakdown. You can create per-route quotas to limit exposure.
[07:18] [console view; Jordan highlights per-route quota]
[07:25] Samir: Can we set quotas per environment (prod vs staging)?
[07:29] Jordan: Yep, per-route and per-key quotas. We also have rate limiting and can configure burst windows.

[07:40] Ana: Another question — how do you do continuous batching? We need to know if short interactive requests suffer from batch-induced latency.
[07:48] Liam: Our runtime does workload-aware batching — it uses adaptive batching windows that try to respect latency SLOs. For interactive low-latency you can set the batch window to small values; Optimize will profile workloads and suggest the best batching profile.
[08:05] Priya: One caveat: batching reduces cost by amortizing setup but can increase tail latency if you accept slightly longer batch windows. That's the classic cost vs latency tradeoff.

[08:20] Mike: Let's talk about errors and idempotency specifics — example response codes and behavior.
[08:25] Priya: 200 means success. 429 is rate-limit: client should backoff. 5xx is transient server error: retry with exponential backoff up to N times. We also return a structured error body with a request_id you can log; that helps our support team match logs.
[08:44] Mike: If a request is partially streamed and you retry, is there a way to request only the tail rather than rerunning full prompt?
[08:52] Liam: Not currently — we don't support resuming mid-generation from an arbitrary token index. Best practice is checkpointing the last confirmed chunk and request the full run if you need final consistency, paired with idempotency to avoid double billing.

[09:08] Ana: For cost control — can Optimize recommend smaller model variants automatically?
[09:14] Priya: Yes, Optimize looks at latency and quality for your prompt set and can suggest quantization and model recommendations. It can also suggest caching prefix completions for common prompts to reduce calls.

[09:30] Mike: Any gotchas with streaming and mobile clients? Mobile networks are flaky.
[09:35] Priya: Mobile is common. Use short-lived streaming and robust reconnect logic; consider sending the full prompt and a client-side checksum to detect partials. If mobile is high-priority, a dedicated capacity plan can give you stronger SLAs.

[09:50] Becky: On data residency — can hosted keep data in EU only?
[09:55] Jordan: Yes, we have region-aware routing and can keep traffic in specific cloud regions. For strict residency we recommend Private deployment.

[10:05] [Demo continues — Priya shows request/response logs and example metrics] 

[10:40] Priya: Quick note on streaming chunk sizes — models sometimes emit punctuation or whitespace as separate deltas, so UI glue logic should coalesce whitespace and filter incomplete tokens. This avoids flicker.

[11:00] Ana: How do you handle model upgrades/rollouts? Concerned about regressions on quality when the model behind the API changes.
[11:07] Jordan: We support pinned model versions and rollout policies. You can pin to a specific model version for the POC; Console supports canary rollouts and A/B. We also have eval tools to run prompt sets and compare outputs automatically.

[11:30] Samir: For the POC we need to run some latency benchmarks in our network. Can you provide a script or reference harness?
[11:36] Priya: Absolutely — I'll share a small harness that hits the streaming endpoint with concurrency control. It includes token accounting and a simple retry wrapper.

[11:46] Mike: Any limit on tokens per request? We have long conversation contexts sometimes into several thousand tokens.
[11:51] Priya: Hosted supports multiple context windows — typical curated models are 4k/8k/32k etc. There's a hard cap per model which we can share. Large contexts increase compute and cost; Optimize suggests truncation/prefix caching strategies.

[12:10] Becky: About KMS and key management — do you integrate with our cloud KMS?
[12:15] Liam: Yes, we support customer-managed keys via KMS for Private deployments and some enterprise hosted tiers. We'll include the KMS integration doc in the followup.

[12:30] [00:12:30] Demo: showing a failed stream and retry sequence with idempotency-key header
[12:46] Priya: See here — when a 502 happens mid-stream our client retries with the same idempotency-key; server returns final result if available. If not, it may start a new run.
[13:02] Ana: You mentioned dedup is "best-effort" on server side. Can you elaborate?
[13:08] Liam: Server keeps a short-lived idempotency mapping for completed runs. It's best-effort because we don't persist indefinitely — that's why client-side dedup plus your own transaction logs are recommended for strict guarantees.

[13:30] Jordan: Let's touch on safety — content filtering and moderation. Hosted APIs offer safety filters that can be applied at request-time. We also provide user-level classification and can flag outputs for manual review.
[13:45] Becky: Are filters customizable per customer? We need the ability to tune thresholds for clinical context.
[13:50] Priya: We have parameterized filters and also the option to plug in a custom filter checkpoint in Private deployments. For hosted we can tune thresholds — in the follow-up we'll map your use cases to filter settings.

[14:05] Mike: One more technical — how does KV cache mention map to streaming? We sometimes reuse context across turns.
[14:13] Liam: The KV cache (sometimes seen in logs as K-V) stores intermediate key-values for decoder layers; when you do chat-turns we can warm cache for subsequent calls. However, cache warming benefits dedicated/private deployments more since they allow persistent workers; hosted may use pooled workers so cache hits are less deterministic.

[14:35] Ana: For the POC, we need samples showing tokenization edge cases and stop sequence splitting.
[14:41] Priya: We'll provide a short doc with examples and suggested stop patterns.

[15:00] [00:15:00] Jordan: Time check — we've hit about 15 minutes demo; we still have retries, backoff code sample, and security Qs. Anything high priority?
[15:10] Mike: Retry sample and the benchmark harness, plus security docs.
[15:14] Jordan: Noted.

[15:20] Priya: I'll quickly paste a pseudo-code retry snippet into chat: exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency-key header, 3 max retries for 5xx, 429 with Retry-After respect. Also how we include request_id in error body for tracing.
[15:38] [Priya posts code snippet in chat]
[15:45] Samir: For tracing, do you support open telemetry headers?
[15:49] Liam: We accept traceparent and baggage headers; Console can ingest traces for correlation.

[16:05] Becky: Are there any legal or procurement quirks for hosted? e.g., data processing agreement, BAA?

[16:11] Jordan: We have standard DPA and can sign BAA for health customers; for stricter needs Private deployments are the route. Procurement often asks for SOC2 evidence which we'll share.

[16:25] Ana: Can we rate-limit per-user to avoid one rogue client burning throughput?

[16:30] Jordan: Yes, per-key and per-user quotaing. We discourage using a single key across many users; instead create sub-keys or route through a gateway with user mapping.

[16:45] Priya: Quick note on token metrics — Console can show token spend per user and per-route in near real time. That helps spot anomalies and tune quotas.

[17:00] Mike: Ok this is helpful. For the POC success criteria: sub-200ms p95 for 100-token summaries and no PHI in logs, plus cost under a threshold. We'll define exact numbers and share.

[17:12] Jordan: Perfect. We'll follow up with pricing, security docs, and the benchmark harness.

[17:20] Becky: One last: where do you store audit logs and can we ship them to our SIEM?
[17:25] Liam: Yes — audit logs can be exported to your S3/GCS or streamed to SIEM via our integrations.

[17:35] [closing demo]
[17:42] Priya: Any other technical questions?
[17:45] Ana: Not right now.

[17:50] Jordan: Alright we'll wrap up with a short recap.

Recap:
- Provide pricing + prompt set (Jordan)
- Share streaming benchmark harness and retry pseudo-code (Priya)
- Provide SOC2 and security whitepaper + KMS integration doc (Jordan/Liam)
- Customer to confirm POC stakeholders and target success metrics (Mike)

[18:20] Mike: Thanks everyone — we'll look out for the materials and propose times for the POC scoping.
[18:27] Jordan: Thanks Valora team, talk soon.

Notes on transcription quality: some punctuation/brand names may be misrecognized (e.g., "K-V cache" vs "KV cache", "V-P-C" vs "VPC", SAML sometimes transcribed as "sample").

End of transcript.
